exp.1:20:
This verse says that believers were called to endure patiently when they do good and receive unjust mistreatment. Christ also suffered for us and left us an example. To follow his steps means to walk the same path He walked, imitating the way He responded. To suffer means to undergo pain or hardship.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians who lived as strangers and suffered rejection. In this passage he speaks especially to servants, though the principle applies to everyone. He wants to encourage them: suffering for doing good pleases God. Then he presents Christ as the model, for He committed no sin, did not return insults, and trusted in God, the righteous judge.

Today, when someone treats you badly without cause, before you respond with anger or revenge, stop and pray. Ask yourself how Jesus would respond. Choose to speak with respect, keep doing good, and leave the matter in God's hands.
exp.0:17:
He says that God redeemed us, that is, set us free by paying a price. He rescued us from a vain way of life, one empty of purpose and lasting value. That way of living had been inherited from our ancestors, from customs passed down to us. And the price was not gold or silver, things that wear out or lose their value over time.

The apostle Peter writes to scattered Christians who felt like foreigners in this world. He has just asked them to live in holiness and reverence toward God. Here he gives them the reason: they were redeemed at an enormous cost, which the next verse explains, the blood of Christ.

For today: when what you inherited weighs on you, whether habits, fears, or empty traditions, remember that your life has a value that God paid for with Christ. Live with gratitude, and ask Him for help in letting go of what does not give life.
exp.4:9:
This verse says that God is the source of all grace, that is, of all the favor and help we do not deserve. He called us to share his eternal glory through Jesus Christ. After you have suffered for a little while, God himself will do four things: he will make you perfect (he will complete and restore you), he will confirm you (he will give you firmness), he will strengthen you (he will make you strong), and he will settle you (he will place you on a secure foundation).

The apostle Peter is speaking. He is writing to Christians who were enduring trials and rejection because of their faith. He has just warned them that the devil is looking for someone to devour, and he asks them to resist, standing firm. Now he encourages them: the suffering is temporary, and God is still at work in them.

For today: when you go through a difficulty, do not think that God has abandoned you. Pray asking him for strength for each day, and remember that he is shaping you and sustaining you until the end.
exp.3:1:
It says that the time we still have left in this body should no longer be spent following the disordered desires of people, but doing what God wants. The word "lusts" refers to strong desires for what displeases God.

The speaker is Peter, an apostle of Jesus, writing to Christians who were suffering mockery and rejection. He reminds them that Christ suffered for them and that they should have the same attitude. Since they had once lived like their pagan neighbors, those neighbors now were surprised by their change and insulted them.

For today: each morning you can ask yourself, "What does God want from me today?" and choose one concrete decision, even if others do not understand it. You do not live to please everyone, but to please God with his help.
exp.1:24:
For you were like sheep that had wandered away and did not know how to find your way back. But now you have returned to Jesus, whom Peter calls the Shepherd and Guardian of your souls. The word "Guardian" here means one who looks after and watches over with careful attention.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians who were suffering because of their faith. He has just spoken of Christ, who suffered without repaying evil with evil and bore our sins on the cross. The image of the sheep recalls Isaiah 53:6. Peter wants to encourage them: Jesus not only suffered for them, he also cares for them today.

For today: if you feel lost, tired, or guilty, you can return to Jesus with confidence. He seeks you and watches over you. Tell him today in prayer where you have strayed, and let him guide you.
exp.3:8:
He says we should welcome others into our homes, one to another, with joy and without complaining. Quejas or grudging comments made under the breath are what he means by complaining. [Note: the reader's verse says "without grudging"; I'll rewrite the glossary sentences accordingly.]

Let me restate that carefully, using only the verse's wording:

He says we should welcome others into our homes, one to another, with joy and without grudging. To grudge means to give or serve reluctantly, with resentment, complaining quietly to yourself.

The speaker is the apostle Peter, and he writes to scattered Christians who were under pressure because of their faith. He tells them the end is near, so they must live with sobriety, prayer, and deep love. In that time, Christian travelers depended heavily on the hospitality of other believers. That is why hospitality was a concrete form of love.

For today: open your home or your table to someone this week, perhaps a brother or sister from church, a neighbor, or someone who is alone. Do it simply and with a good attitude, without grudging, even if it is not perfect.
exp.2:15:
It says we should keep a clear conscience, that is, live uprightly before God. Thus, when people speak badly of us and accuse us of doing wrong, those who insult our good way of living in Christ will be put to shame.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians who were suffering rejection and mockery because of their faith. He asks them to respond with gentleness and respect, without fear. Their sincere lives were meant to support their words, even when they were criticized unjustly. Then he reminds them that Christ also suffered though He was innocent.

For today: if someone criticizes you or speaks badly of you because of your faith, do not respond in anger. Examine your heart, try to live with honesty, and treat everyone with kindness. Over time, your conduct can be the best witness.
exp.1:18:
It says that God is pleased when a person endures pains and mistreatment they do not deserve, and it does so because their conscience is set on God. The word "pleasing" here means that the person has God's favor. "Grief" refers to pains or sufferings, and "suffering wrongfully" means suffering without having done anything wrong.

Peter writes to Christians who lived as foreigners and were looked down on because of their faith. Here he speaks to servants, people who worked under masters, sometimes harsh ones. He does not approve of injustice; he encourages acting with integrity and trusting God. Right after this, he points to Christ, who suffered though innocent, as an example.

For today: if you are treated badly at work or at home even though you act honestly, do not answer with revenge or deceit. Keep doing what is right before God and pray for wisdom. If the abuse is serious, seeking help and protection is also wise.
exp.0:15:
This verse says that God asks us to be holy because He is holy. Peter is quoting the Scriptures. To be holy means to be set apart for God, pure, and dedicated to Him. The quotation comes from the law of Moses, in the book of Leviticus.

Peter writes to believers who are scattered and live as foreigners in lands not their own. He reminds them that they should no longer live by the desires they had before, when they did not know God. As obedient children, they should resemble their Father. Here, the word for conduct means behavior or the way a person lives.

For today: holiness is not only avoiding what is wrong, but resembling God in everyday life. Today, choose one small decision, such as how you speak or how you treat someone, and ask God to help you make it in a way that reflects Him.
exp.2:16:
It says that, if a believer happens to suffer, it is better to suffer for doing what is right than for doing what is wrong. "Suffer" is the word that matters here, meaning to endure pain or hardship. The phrase about the will of God recognizes that God allows that suffering and does not ignore it.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians who lived surrounded by people who criticized them and accused them of doing wrong. He asks them to respond with gentleness, with a clear conscience, and without returning evil for evil. Right after this, he gives Christ as an example, who suffered though he was righteous, in order to bring us to God.

For today: if people criticize you or treat you badly for acting with honesty and kindness, do not lose heart or respond with revenge. Examine your conscience, keep doing good, and trust that God sees what you are going through and can use it for his good purposes.
exp.3:17:
This verse says that for the righteous, being saved is hard or difficult, and so it asks what will become of those who do not believe or obey God. The phrase "scarcely" does not mean that God is unwilling to save; it means that the path includes trials.

The apostle Peter is writing to Christians who are suffering for their faith. He explains that suffering is not a sign that God has abandoned them, but part of a process in which God purifies his people. If God is serious about his own, how much more will he be serious about those who reject the gospel.

For today: if you are going through trials because you follow Christ, do not lose heart or feel ashamed. Trust in God, keep doing good, and place your life in his hands.
exp.1:9:
This verse says that believers, in the past, were not a people of their own and had not received God's mercy. Now they are God's people and have received his mercy. The phrase "had obtained mercy" means that God showed them compassion and forgiveness.

Here the apostle Peter is speaking, and he is writing to scattered Christians who felt like foreigners. He reminds them of their new identity in Christ. His words resemble those of the prophet Hosea, who spoke about Israel. Peter now applies them to everyone who believes, whether they were Jews or not. He calls them to live in a way that honors God.

Today, if you feel alone, without a place, or burdened by guilt, remember that God receives you through his mercy. Live with gratitude and seek out other believers, so that together you can show his goodness.
exp.2:12:
What it says: Peter asks an encouraging question: who will harm you if you devote yourselves to doing good? "Harm" means to hurt or do evil to someone. The question assumes that someone who lives doing good should not normally receive evil.

Context: The apostle Peter is speaking to Christians who lived as strangers and were viewed with suspicion. He has just quoted Psalm 34 about seeking peace and trusting that God cares for the righteous. He then clarifies that, even if they suffer for doing good, they are blessed, that is, happy. So he does not promise that there will never be harm, but that nothing can take away what God gives them. Some understand it this way; others see it as a general principle.

For today: Keep doing good even when people don't thank you, and place your security in God's hands, without living in fear.
exp.1:2:
If you have tasted, that is, experienced, that the Lord is good and kind, then you have reason to desire his Word. "If so be" means "if indeed," and here it carries the sense of "if, as you have found." "Gracious" means kind, tender and full of grace. It is a phrase that alludes to Psalm 34:8.

The apostle Peter speaks to scattered and suffering Christians. He has just asked them to put away malice, deceit and envy, and to long for spiritual milk as newborn babies do. Here he gives them the reason: they have already known the goodness of the Lord. Then he presents Christ as the living stone.

For today: when weariness or routine cools your desire to pray and read the Bible, remember the times God has shown you his goodness. That memory awakens the hunger to return to him.
exp.3:7:
He says that, above all, we should love one another with a deep and steady love. "Charity" here means love (in Greek, agápe), and "fervent" means that it keeps working at it and does not grow cold. "Will cover a multitude of sins" means that this love forgives the faults of others instead of exposing them.

The apostle Peter speaks to Christians who were suffering rejection because of their faith. He reminds them that the end is near, so they should live with calm, pray, and take care of one another. Some think the phrase resembles Proverbs 10:12; it does not mean that love buys God's forgiveness, but that it forgives the offenses between brothers and sisters.

For today: when someone in your family or your church fails you, decide to forgive and do not go telling others about it. Pray for that person and seek them out with kindness.
exp.3:10:
If anyone speaks, they should do so as one who passes on the words of God, that is, faithfully to what God has said. Whoever serves should do it with the strength that God supplies. The aim is that God be glorified in all things, through Jesus Christ.

The apostle Peter writes to scattered Christians who faced rejection and suffering. Before speaking of trials, he reminds them how to live as a community: with hospitality, and using each gift for the good of others. He closes this passage with praise to God.

For today: before you speak or serve, pray and ask God for his strength and guidance. Then, whether you teach, help, cook, or listen to someone, you can do it without pride or exhaustion, seeking that God be honored and not you.
exp.1:17:
This verse says that servants should respect and submit to their masters with reverence, not only to the kind and fair ones, but also to the harsh or severe ones. "Servants" here means household slaves. The word "submit" means to put oneself under someone's authority. "Fear" speaks of respect, especially before God. The harsh ones are unjust or difficult masters.

The apostle Peter writes to scattered Christians who live as strangers in a hostile world. He asks them for an exemplary conduct that honors God. Peter does not approve of slavery; he addresses people who were within that system, and he gives them Christ as an example of unjust suffering (in the following verses).

For today: in a job with a difficult boss, we can fulfill our duties with honesty and respect, without returning evil for evil, and work as for God. This does not mean keeping silent in the face of abuse; seeking justice and protection is also right.
exp.2:4:
This verse says that the holy women of old, who trusted in God, adorned themselves in the way Peter has just described: with a beautiful character on the inside. Part of that adornment was being in subjection to their own husbands, that is, respectfully yielding to them.

Peter, an apostle of Jesus, writes to Christians who were under pressure because of their faith. Here he addresses wives, some of whom had husbands who did not believe. He shows them that their true worth does not depend on outward appearance, and he gives them the example of women from the Old Testament, such as Sarah. Christians understand differently how this submission should be applied today, but all agree that Peter is speaking of a humble spirit that trusts in God.

For today: take care of your heart first, cultivating peace, kindness, and trust in God, rather than your image before others.
exp.2:6:
This verse says that husbands should live with their wives with understanding, treating them with respect. It calls the woman the "weaker vessel," which is usually understood as a reference to physical strength, not to value or ability. It makes clear that both are "heirs together of the grace of life," that is, equal before God. If the husband does not do this, his prayers may be hindered, or obstructed.

Peter writes to Christians who were under pressure because of their faith. Earlier he spoke to wives; now he addresses husbands. In that time the man held great power in the home, and Peter calls him to use it with care and honor.

For today: really listen to your partner, try to understand their needs, and treat them with respect, since the way you live together affects your relationship with God.
exp.0:14:
He says that God, who called us, is holy, and therefore we too must be holy in all our manner of living. The word "conversation" here does not refer only to speaking, but to our whole conduct, the way we live each day. "Holy" means set apart for God and resembling his character.

Peter writes to scattered Christians who faced rejection because of their faith. Earlier he asked them to think clearly and obey God, without returning to the desires of their former life. Then, in the next verse, he cites the ancient Scripture (Leviticus) to support this call: God is holy, and his people must reflect it.

Today, holiness begins by remembering that God has called us. Think of one area of your routine, such as your work, your words, or your decisions in private, and ask him for help to act there in a way that honors him.
exp.0:10:
This verse says that the prophets of the Old Testament studied very carefully what time and what moment the Spirit of Christ, who was in them, was pointing to. That Spirit announced to them in advance two things: the sufferings Christ would go through and the glory that would come after.

Peter is writing to Christians who were suffering and living as scattered strangers. He wants to encourage them by showing that their salvation was expected and longed for by the prophets. He also reminds them that Christ's path was first pain and then glory. How and when everything would be fulfilled, the prophets did not fully understand.

For today: if you are going through a trial, remember that God has not forgotten you. Christ's suffering ended in glory, and that hope is yours too. Trust that God works with purpose, even when you do not yet understand everything.
exp.0:9:
It says that the prophets of the Old Testament spoke about the grace God would give to believers, and that they worked hard to understand that salvation.

Peter writes to Christians who were suffering for their faith and had been scattered. He wants to encourage them by showing that their salvation is so precious that the prophets longed to understand it. What those prophets only saw from a distance, these believers had now received through Christ. According to the verses that follow, the Spirit of Christ spoke to them about his sufferings and the glory that would come after.

For today: do not take your salvation for granted. If the prophets searched with such desire for what you already know, open your Bible with gratitude and hunger, and ask God to show you more of Christ.
exp.4:7:
It says we should be sober, that is, think calmly and clearly, and stay awake and alert. The reason is that the devil, our enemy, goes about like a roaring lion, looking for someone to devour. "Be sober" means to be self-controlled and balanced; "be vigilant" means to stay watchful.

Peter writes to Christians who were suffering pressure and hardship because of their faith. Just before this, he asked them to be humble and to cast their worries on God, who cares for them. Then he tells them to resist, standing firm in the faith, and reminds them that their fellow believers go through the same things. He closes by promising that God himself will strengthen them.

For today: do not live distracted or afraid. Each day, bring your anxieties to God in prayer, stay alert to whatever pulls you away from him, and lean on the community of believers to resist firmly.
exp.2:3:
This verse says that true beauty is not found in what shows on the outside, but in "the hidden man of the heart," that is, in the inner person, the one that only God sees fully. Beauty that does not spoil or fade is the kind that lasts. A spirit that is gentle and peaceful is a kind and calm character. God values this very highly.

The apostle Peter wrote to Christians who lived as a minority, sometimes looked down on. Here he speaks to wives, and some had husbands who did not believe. He teaches them that a clean and respectful life can speak louder than words. Some scholars see here a teaching for everyone, not only for women.

Today we can care for the heart as much as for appearance. Before answering in anger, let us ask God for calm and a kind manner.
exp.3:11:
Beloved, the verse says, the believers whom Peter addresses should not be surprised when they go through intense suffering. The image of being tested by fire is a picture: just as fire tests and purifies metal, suffering tests faith. The phrase "strange thing" means something unusual or outside the ordinary.

Peter, an apostle of Jesus, writes to scattered Christians who faced rejection and mockery for following Christ. The verses before this one speak of serving one another so that God is glorified. The verses after it say that suffering for Christ is a reason for joy. Scholars debate how severe the persecution was at that time, but the suffering was real.

For today: when a trial comes, do not think that God has abandoned you. Ask Him for strength, lean on other believers, and remember that He can use that difficulty to strengthen your faith.
exp.1:5:
Peter says that the Scripture had already announced this: God places in Zion a chief cornerstone, that is, the cornerstone that holds up and aligns the whole building. It is chosen and precious. Whoever trusts in it will not be "confounded," that is, put to shame or let down.

Peter writes to Christians who were suffering rejection. He quotes Isaiah 28:16 to show that Christ, although he was rejected by people, is chosen by God. In this way he encourages them: they too are part of that spiritual house built on him.

Today, if you feel rejected or insecure because you follow Jesus, remember that your life rests on the stone God chose. Trusting in Christ is a firm foundation, even when others do not value it.
exp.2:0:
It says that wives should be subject to their own husbands. The goal is that husbands who do not believe the word of God may be won without words, only by the way their wives live. "Conduct" here does not mean talk, but a way of living. "Subject" means to submit with respect and good order.

The apostle Peter is speaking to Christians who were under pressure in a society that did not share their faith. The word "likewise" connects this with what came before, where he asks everyone for an exemplary way of living, following Christ. He addresses these words to women with unbelieving husbands. How to practice submission today is understood in various ways among Christians, but the text emphasizes the witness.

For today: if someone in your family does not share your faith, work to let your patience, your kindness and your integrity speak louder than your arguments or reproaches.
exp.0:21:
This verse says that believers have already been cleansed within by obeying the true message of the gospel, with the help of the Spirit. Because of this, they should now love one another with a sincere affection. "Brotherly love" means the love of brothers and sisters. "Without hypocrisy" means without pretense. "Deeply" means with a profound and intense love, and "a pure heart" speaks of clean intentions.

Peter writes to scattered Christians who were going through trials and rejection. He reminds them that their faith in Christ, risen and glorified, has made them new. Since they have been born again through the word of God (as the text goes on to say), their lives should show that change, above all in how they treat one another. Some understand being "cleansed" as the change that begins at belief, not as complete perfection.

Today, think of a brother or sister in your church with whom you struggle. Do something concrete for that person this week: call them, pray for them, or help them, without expecting anything in return.
exp.4:6:
This verse invites us to hand over to God all our worries. The word "care" in the verse above is the one to hold onto: it means anxiety, concern, or restlessness. To "cast" something is like throwing a heavy load onto someone stronger. The reason is simple: God cares for us.

The apostle Peter is speaking to Christians who were suffering pressure and hostility because of their faith. He has just been talking about humility, and giving up our anxieties is a way of humbling ourselves under God's hand, admitting that we do not control everything. He then warns them to be alert to the devil and to affliction.

Today, when a worry steals your peace, tell it to God in prayer, in detail and with honesty. Then, each time it returns to your mind, hand it over again, trusting that God cares for you.
exp.1:0:
This verse says that whoever follows Christ must leave behind certain attitudes. "Malice" is the desire to do harm. "Deceit" is manipulating others with lies. "Pretense" is hypocrisy, appearing to be what one is not. "Envy" is grief over another's good fortune. "Slander" consists of criticisms and false accusations that damage other people's good name.

The one speaking is the apostle Peter, writing to scattered Christians who were facing rejection. By tradition it is thought he wrote from Rome, though not all scholars affirm this with certainty. The word "therefore" links this with what comes before: since they have been renewed and called to love one another from the heart, they must put aside whatever destroys unity. The next verse completes the thought: instead of those behaviors, they should desire the Word as a newborn baby desires milk.

Today, before speaking about someone who is not present, ask yourself whether you would say it to their face. If not, it is better to keep silent and pray for that person.
exp.1:16:
This verse gives four short commands. "Honour" means to treat with respect and value. We should respect every person, love the brothers and sisters in the faith (the brotherhood is the community of believers), show reverence toward God, and honour the king, that is, the civil authority.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians scattered abroad who lived as strangers and were sometimes looked down on or accused. He asks them for good conduct that would silence unfair criticism. Their freedom in Christ is no excuse for doing wrong, but a way of serving God. That is why he speaks to them about respect for everyone, for the church, and for the authorities.

Today we can practice this verse by treating with respect even someone who thinks differently or someone we do not like. We can pray for our authorities and speak about them without mockery or contempt, while we keep putting God first.
exp.3:4:
This verse says that those who mock believers for no longer living their former disorderly lives will have to give account to God.

Peter writes to Christians who were suffering mockery and rejection because they no longer lived as they once did, in excess and in idolatry. He encourages them by reminding them that the final word does not belong to those who laugh at them, but to God, who is just. Some understand this as a warning and others as a comfort for believers.

For today: when people criticize you for living according to your faith, do not respond with resentment or fear. Trust that God sees everything and judges with justice. Keep doing what is good with humility.
exp.1:14:
This verse says that God wants believers, through a good and honest life, to leave without arguments those who speak without knowledge. The phrase "put to silence" means to silence, and "ignorance" refers to false accusations. "Foolish men" are people who are foolish, who speak without thinking or without basis.

Peter writes to scattered Christians who were living as foreigners in an environment that often looked at them with suspicion and accused them of doing wrong. For this reason he asks them to respect the authorities and to live in an exemplary way. He does not answer with lawsuits or loud defenses, but with conduct that disproves the slander.

Today, when someone speaks badly of you because of your faith, do not rush to argue. Try to be punctual, honest, and kind at work, at home, and in the community. Over time, your good deeds can speak louder than any criticism.
exp.0:1:
It says that the believers were chosen according to what God the Father had already known beforehand (his foreknowledge). This choosing is lived out through the sanctifying work of the Spirit, who sets us apart for God. Its purpose is twofold: to obey Jesus Christ and to be sprinkled with his blood, an image of cleansing and of belonging to the new covenant. It closes with a wish that grace and peace may be multiplied to them, that is, that they may abound more and more.

The apostle Peter speaks to Christians who are strangers, scattered across several regions of what is today Turkey. They were probably suffering rejection because of their faith. Peter reminds them that they are not forgotten: God knows them, chose them, and cares for them. Christians debate how to understand foreknowledge, but here the emphasis is on comfort.

For today: if you feel out of place or tired of being different, remember that God knows you and called you. Ask him today for his peace, and obey him in a concrete decision, trusting in his grace.
exp.1:22:
This verse says that Jesus, when he was insulted, did not answer with insults. When he suffered, he did not threaten anyone. Instead of taking revenge, he entrusted his case to God, who judges with justice. In this verse, "reviled" means to insult or speak with contempt.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians who were suffering injustice, and in this passage he speaks especially to servants who were being mistreated. He presents Christ to them as the example to follow. Peter was close to Jesus and knew well how he responded to suffering. The text then explains that Christ bore our sins on the cross.

For today: when someone offends you, before answering in anger, breathe and pray. Hand the injustice over to God and trust that he knows how to bring about justice. This does not mean always staying silent or accepting abuse, but refusing to repay evil with evil.
exp.1:23:
This verse says that Jesus carried our sins in his own body when he died on the cross ("the tree"). He did this so that we would stop living under sin, as people who have died to it, and would live for what is right and good. "Ye were healed" by his wounds: the word "wounds" points to the blows he suffered. Many understand this healing as forgiveness and the restoration of the soul.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians who were suffering unjustly. Earlier he set Jesus before them as an example: he did not return insults or threats, but trusted in God. Here Peter explains that this suffering had a purpose: to rescue us. Then he calls them sheep who had gone astray and returned to the Shepherd.

For today: if Christ paid for your sin, you do not have to live enslaved to it. Today you can choose one concrete act of righteousness, such as asking forgiveness or acting with honesty, trusting in his grace.
exp.2:21:
This verse says that Jesus Christ is seated at the right hand of God, that is, in the place of honor and authority, after going up into heaven. The angels, the authorities and the powers (beings with authority, and beings of great strength) are made subject to him, meaning they are under his rule.

Peter writes to Christians who were suffering for their faith. He has just spoken of the resurrection of Christ, and of Noah, who was saved in the midst of judgment. Peter shows that Jesus, who also suffered, now reigns over every power. Some details of the earlier passage are interpreted in several ways, but this verse is clear: Christ has the victory.

For today: when you feel fear or pressure for following Jesus, remember that he rules over every force. You can pray with confidence, knowing that your life is in the hands of the Lord, who is the most powerful.
exp.0:20:
This verse says that through Christ you believe in God. It was God who raised him from the dead and gave him glory. Because of this, your faith and hope rest in God. The phrase "and gave him glory" means that God honored him and exalted him.

Peter writes to scattered Christians who were going through trials and living as foreigners. He has just reminded them that Christ, the lamb without blemish, gave his blood for them. Now he shows them that the resurrection confirms that work and gives them a firm basis for trusting God.

When everything seems uncertain, remember that God raised Jesus from the dead. That is a solid reason to trust. Today you can hand God a specific worry and wait on him, knowing that his power and faithfulness were already shown in the resurrection.
exp.4:13:
The verse tells Christians to greet one another with sincere affection, and it wishes God's peace on all who belong to Christ. A kiss was a greeting of affection between believers in the faith.

Peter, the apostle, is speaking as he closes his letter to believers who were suffering for their faith. He has just reminded them that God's grace is firm. He mentions Silvanus, who helped carry the letter, and Mark. Babylon was probably a name for Rome, though some think it was the city itself. Scholars do not fully agree on this.

Today we can look for a warm and concrete way to show affection to someone in our church: a hug, a message, or a visit. In this way the peace of Christ becomes visible among us.
exp.2:11:
This verse says that God watches over the righteous, that is, over those who seek to do what is right. His eyes are on them and his ears are attentive to their prayers, meaning he looks on them with care and listens to them. On the other hand, the face of the Lord is set against those who do evil.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians who were suffering for their faith. Here he quotes Psalm 34, which speaks of loving life, guarding one's words, turning away from evil, and seeking peace. He wants to encourage them to live well even when others treat them badly, because God sees them.

For today: when you feel ignored or treated unfairly, respond with goodness and with sincere words, instead of revenge. Pray with confidence, remembering that God sees you and hears you.
exp.1:1:
This verse invites us to desire spiritual milk the way newborn babies do, with a sincere and natural hunger. The word "pure" here means unmixed and undiluted, with nothing added or corrupted. The word "salvation" in this verse refers to being saved; many translations read "that by it you may grow up into salvation," meaning a mature Christian life.

The apostle Peter is writing to scattered Christians who were under pressure because of their faith. Earlier in the letter he urged them to put away malice, deceit, envy, and slander. Then he reminds them that they have already tasted that the Lord is good, the living stone chosen by God.

For today: just as a baby looks for food every day, look for a daily time to read the Bible with a simple heart. Ask God to teach you and to help you let go of whatever harms your relationships.
exp.3:14:
This verse says that no believer should suffer for having done something wrong, such as murder, theft, or wrongdoing. It also mentions being a busybody in other people's matters, that is, interfering in affairs that are not one's own. The verse's word for the kind of person who does evil is one who does wrong, and the verse's own words are used for these ideas.

Peter writes to Christians who were suffering for following Jesus. He had already told them that suffering for Christ is a reason for joy. Now he clarifies that not all suffering is honorable: if someone suffers because of their own bad conduct, that does not honor God. The phrase about being a busybody in other people's matters is uncommon in the original Greek, and it is understood in several ways, such as gossiping, meddling in the lives of others, or acting as an unauthorized overseer.

For today: before we complain about a difficulty, let us ask ourselves honestly whether we caused it. Let us guard our conduct, including our tongue and improper curiosity, so that if we suffer, it is only for faithfulness to Christ.
exp.4:3:
This verse says that when Jesus Christ appears, the one called here "the chief Shepherd," those who have faithfully cared for his people will receive a reward. The word "appear" in the verse above is the same idea as the word "appears" here. A "crown that fadeth not away" is a reward that never wilts or ends. "Glory" speaks of the honor that comes from God.

Peter writes to Christians who were suffering because of their faith. Just before this verse, he encourages the elders or leaders of the churches to care for the flock willingly, without seeking money and without ruling harshly. Jesus is the main shepherd, and the leaders are his helpers. Peter reminds them that their reward comes from Christ, not from people.

For today: if you care for others in your family, church, or workplace, do it with kindness and without seeking applause. God sees what no one else sees.
exp.3:12:
This verse says that, instead of being frightened by suffering, we can rejoice in sharing in what Christ suffered. "Rejoice" is the word for being glad. "Partakers" means having a share in something. The reason is that when Jesus appears in his glory, we will also be glad with an overflowing joy.

Peter writes to Christians who were suffering mockery and rejection for following Jesus. He calls them dear friends and tells them that the trial, which he compares to a fire, is not something strange or unusual. Their suffering for Christ is not a sign of being abandoned, but of union with him. Peter himself was a witness to the sufferings of Jesus.

For today: if you are criticized or excluded for living your faith honestly, do not think that God has forgotten you. Ask him to give you peace and hope, and remember that Christ knows that pain and walks with you.
exp.0:13:
This verse says that Christians, as obedient children of God, should no longer let themselves be shaped by the wrong desires that once controlled them. "Not conforming yourselves" means not taking on the same pattern or way of life. "Ignorance" refers to the time when they did not know God or his will.

The apostle Peter writes to believers who were scattered, many of them likely under pressure and suffering. He has just reminded them of the salvation that was announced to them, and he calls them to live with a clear, alert mind and to stand firm in hope. This verse prepares the next call: to be holy, because God is holy.

For today: think of a habit or desire that once guided your life and still pulls you backward. Today, pray about that specific point, and take one simple step to obey God in it, without relying only on your own strength.
exp.2:18:
He says that Christ, after being "made alive in the spirit," went and proclaimed to "the spirits in prison." The word "went" is in the verse, and "proclaimed" appears in the same verse, so there is no need to explain them. The text clarifies that these were the people who disobeyed in the days of Noah.

Peter writes to Christians who suffer for doing good. He reminds them that Christ also suffered though he was righteous, and that God raised him up. This passage is difficult and is interpreted in several ways: that Christ spoke through Noah to his contemporaries, that he proclaimed victory to fallen spiritual beings, or that he announced something to the dead. There is no complete agreement. What is clear is the message: Christ triumphs.

If you suffer for doing what is right, you are not alone or defeated. Like Noah, who was faithful even though few followed him, you can trust that God sustains his people and Christ has already won.
exp.1:3:
It tells us that we should come close to Jesus Christ, whom Peter calls a "living stone." The word "coming" means drawing near to him, and "disallowed" means rejected. Men rejected him, but God chose him and regards him as very precious.

Peter writes to Christians who were suffering contempt for their faith. He has just spoken to them about growing like infants who long for spiritual milk. Now he uses the image of a stone to show that Jesus, though he was rejected, is the foundation of God's house. The verses that follow quote the Old Testament to support this idea.

For today: if the world rejects you or looks down on you for following Christ, remember that God values Him, and you in Him. Draw near to Jesus every day in prayer and Bible reading, and let Him be your security.
exp.0:8:
This verse says that believers are receiving the goal of their faith: the salvation of their souls. The word "health" here is an old way of saying "salvation." "Receiving" means reaching or obtaining. In other words, faith is not left without fruit; it arrives at a destination.

The apostle Peter writes to scattered Christians who were suffering trials and pressure for following Jesus. He reminds them that their difficulties prove their faith, just as fire tests gold. Although they have not seen Christ, they love him and rejoice. The ancient prophets also longed to understand this salvation, which they now enjoy.

For today: when you go through difficult moments, remember that your faith in Christ has a secure destination. Trials are not the end of the story. Ask God to help you look beyond the problem and trust the salvation he gives you.
exp.2:1:
This verse says that husbands who do not believe will see the way their wives live. "Chaste" means pure, clean, and wholesome. "Conduct" is not just speech, but all of one's behavior, the way one lives. "Fear" here is understood as respect and reverence toward God.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians who were under pressure in a society that did not share their faith. He speaks to wives who were married to unbelieving men. His idea is that a testimony of a pure and respectful life can speak louder than arguments or reproaches.

For today: if you want someone close to you to come to know God, work to make your conduct honest, kind, and consistent. Rather than pressing with words, let your daily life show the character of Christ, and pray for that person with patience.
exp.0:16:
If you call on God as Father, remember that He judges everyone impartially, without favoritism, according to what each person does. So "pass the time in fear" means living with respect and reverence toward God. "Conduct" in this text means behavior or the way one lives. "Sojourning" is the time we spend here as foreigners passing through.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians who are scattered and sometimes mistreated for their faith. He reminds them that God called them to be holy. Their closeness to God as Father is no excuse for living carelessly. What follows explains why: they were redeemed with the precious blood of Christ, a very high price.

Today, we can live each day with gratitude and respect toward God. Before deciding something at work, at home, or with money, ask yourself: "Does this honor my Father, who redeemed me with such love?"
exp.4:5:
It says we should humble ourselves, that is, recognize that we depend on God and place ourselves under his authority. The "mighty hand of God" speaks of his strength and his care. To "exalt" means to lift up or honor. And "in due time" means at the moment God considers right, not when we want it.

Peter, an apostle of Jesus, writes to Christians who were suffering pressure and rejection because of their faith. Earlier he had urged mutual submission and humility, because God opposes the proud. Then he encourages them to hand over their anxieties to him and to stay alert in the face of the devil. Humility here is a way of trusting God in the middle of trial.

Today, when you feel ignored or pressured, instead of fighting for your place, pray and give your concern to God. Serve with patience, and trust that he knows when and how to lift you up.
exp.2:8:
This verse asks us not to answer evil with more evil, or insults with insults. Instead, we are to bless, that is, to wish and do good to the person who treats us badly. The word "railing" here means hurtful words or insults. And the phrase "that ye should inherit a blessing" means that God called us to receive his blessing as a gift.

Peter, an apostle of Jesus, writes to Christians who lived as strangers and suffered rejection. He has already spoken to them about how to live at home and among fellow believers. Now he sums up: be united and compassionate, and do not repay evil with evil. The verses that follow quote a psalm that invites us to seek peace.

Today, when someone offends you, at home, at work, or online, pause before you respond. Answer with calm, or pray for that person. Blessing someone does not mean approving of the harm done, but trusting that God takes care of you.
exp.0:2:
Peter praises God, whom he calls the Father of Jesus Christ. He says that, because of his great mercy, God has caused us to be born again ("regenerated"), and that this new birth gives us a living hope, that is, a firm hope that does not die. That hope rests on the fact that Jesus rose from the dead.

Peter, an apostle of Jesus, writes to Christians scattered as strangers across several regions of Asia Minor. Many of them were going through hardships, so he begins by reminding them of what God has already done for them. The verses that follow speak of an inheritance kept secure in heaven.

For today: when you feel tired or see no way out, remember that your hope does not depend on your circumstances, but on the fact that Christ lives. Thank God today for his mercy and rest in that hope.
exp.1:6:
This verse says that Jesus, the stone chosen by God, is a source of honor and value for those who believe in him. But for those who do not obey, that same stone that the builders rejected became the main stone of the building. "Cornerstone" is the stone at the corner, which holds up and lines up the whole structure. "Disobedient" refers to those who refuse to believe and follow the message.

Peter writes to Christians scattered abroad who were suffering rejection because of their faith. He quotes the Old Testament (Isaiah 28:16 and Psalm 118:22) to encourage them: even though many despise Christ, God honored him. Some interpreters debate the meaning of the phrase "for which they were appointed" in the following verse, and they understand it in different ways.

Today, if you feel rejected for following Jesus, remember that God values what the world despises. Rely on Christ as your firm foundation and do not be ashamed of him.
exp.2:5:
It says that Sarah respected her husband Abraham, even calling him "lord," which was a polite way of addressing him. Peter says that Christian women are Sarah's "daughters" when they do good and do not let fear control them.

Peter writes to Christians who were under pressure because of their faith. Earlier he speaks of inner beauty, and here he holds up Sarah as an example of women who trusted in God. The reference to calling him "lord" points to Genesis 18:12. Scholars debate how much of this was the custom of her time and how much is lasting teaching. Peter then also urges husbands to honor their wives.

For today: do good with a calm spirit and trust God instead of acting out of fear. Treat others, at home and outside it, with respect and kindness.
exp.3:18:
It says that those who suffer because God allows it or wills it within his plan should entrust their lives to him, trusting in him as a faithful Creator. And in the meantime, they should keep doing good.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians who were suffering rejection and persecution for their faith. Earlier he spoke of God's judgment beginning with his people, to purify them. If that is serious for believers, it will be all the more so for those who reject the gospel. Here he closes with a word of comfort and guidance.

Today, when you go through a trial, do not hold on only to worry. Pray, handing over your situation and your heart to God, and keep acting with honesty and kindness, even when others treat you badly.
exp.3:16:
This verse says that the time has come for God to examine and correct his people, that is, the believers. If God begins with his own, the end of those who reject the gospel will be much more serious. "Judgment" here speaks of an evaluation that purifies; "house of God" refers to the community of believers.

Peter writes to Christians who were suffering for following Jesus. He tells them not to suffer for doing wrong, but, if it is for being Christians, not to be ashamed. Many understand that trials refine faith, though some also see here a broader judgment of God. Both ideas fit the context.

Today, when you go through difficulties, do not lose heart right away. Examine your life with humility, entrust your soul to God, who is faithful, and keep doing good.
exp.2:14:
Peter says we should set apart God as holy deep within our being, giving him first place. He also asks us to always be ready to answer anyone who asks why we have hope. Here, "ready" means prepared, and gentleness is a humble and kind way of treating others. "Respect" here can be understood as reverence, whether toward God or toward the person who asks.

The apostle Peter writes to scattered Christians who were suffering mockery and rejection because of their faith. Shortly before, he told them not to fear their opponents. Then he reminds them to keep a good conscience, so that those who accuse them will be put to shame when they see their good conduct in Christ.

For today: if someone asks you about your faith, do not argue or defend yourself with pride. Instead, spend time with God so that He governs your heart, and then explain simply and kindly why you put your hope in Christ.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that believers rejoice because of the hope of their inheritance in heaven, even though now, for a little while, they suffer various trials. The word "temptations" here means trials or difficulties, not only a desire to sin. The phrase "if necessary" indicates that God allows those trials for a purpose.

The one speaking is the apostle Peter. He writes to scattered Christians who were facing suffering and rejection because of their faith. He wants to encourage them by reminding them that their hope is secure and that their trials have an end and a value, as he explains in the following verse.

For today: when you go through a difficulty, you do not have to pretend it does not hurt. You can weep and at the same time have joy, because you know that God keeps you and that your present suffering is not the end of the story.
exp.0:11:
This verse says that God revealed to the prophets of the Old Testament that their messages were not only for themselves, but for the believers who would come later. Those truths have now been announced by those who preached the gospel with the power of the Holy Spirit, sent down from heaven. The word "ministered" means that they served or passed on the message. Even the angels long to look closely into this salvation.

Peter writes to scattered Christians who were suffering for their faith. He wants to encourage them by reminding them that the salvation they have is something great, announced long ago, with the sufferings and glory of Christ. What they are living through today is part of a plan of God that comes from far back.

Today, when the gospel may seem ordinary or dull to you, remember that prophets waited for it and angels gaze at it with wonder. Read it with gratitude, and live with the seriousness and joy of someone who has received a treasure.
exp.0:3:
It says God has given us an inheritance that is never damaged. "Incorruptible" means it does not rot or get destroyed. Nothing can make it dirty or stain it. Nothing can make it fade, the way a flower loses its beauty and dries up. And it is kept in heaven: God guards it carefully for us.

Peter, one of Jesus' apostles, writes to scattered Christians who were suffering trials and pressure because of their faith. Before speaking of their pains, he reminds them of what they have in Christ: a living hope, based on the resurrection of Jesus. The verses that follow say that God himself guards them with his power.

For today: when you lose something or suffer, remember that the most precious thing you have in Christ does not depend on this world. Rest in the knowledge that God guards your inheritance and also guards you.
exp.3:9:
This verse says that every believer has received a gift from God, or an ability to serve, and should use it to benefit others. "Administer it" means putting it at the service of others. "Stewards" are managers who take care of and distribute what does not belong to them. "Manifold grace" here refers to the different gifts God gives.

The one speaking is Peter, writing to scattered Christians who faced rejection and suffering. Just before, he speaks of loving one another deeply and opening the home without complaint. Afterward he clarifies that whoever speaks or serves should do so with the strength God provides, so that God may be glorified. Scholars understand "gift" broadly: it can include talents, hospitality, or teaching.

Today, ask yourself what you have received: time, skill, money, or encouragement. Choose to do something concrete this week for someone in your church or family, without boasting, trusting in the strength God gives you.
exp.2:13:
It says that if someone suffers for doing good, God calls them "blessed," that is, happy or favored. For this reason, believers should not be afraid of those who threaten them, nor let themselves be shaken, which means being overcome by anguish or losing their composure. The phrase "their fear" can be understood as fear of the threats of the opponents.

Peter is writing to scattered Christians who faced rejection and mockery because of their faith. Earlier he said that God watches over the righteous and hears their prayers. Here he makes clear that, although doing good sometimes brings suffering, God does not abandon them. Some understand this to refer to social pressures, and others to stronger persecution; the text does not specify more.

For today: if people criticize you or leave you out for acting with honesty, do not respond with fear. Do what is right with calm, and pray to God for the peace you need.
exp.2:17:
It says that Christ suffered once for sins. He, who is just, died in place of us, who are unjust, to bring us near to God. He was put to death in the body, but was made alive again by the Spirit. Some understand "by the Spirit" as the Holy Spirit, others as his risen state.

Peter writes to Christians who were suffering mockery and accusations for following Jesus. He tells them it is better to suffer for doing good than for doing evil. To encourage them, he points to Christ: He also suffered though innocent, and his suffering had a glorious purpose. The verses that follow are difficult and are interpreted in several ways.

If today you suffer for acting with honesty and kindness, you are not alone. Christ has already gone through that and opened the way to God for you. Keep doing good with peace, trusting in Him.
exp.2:7:
It says that all believers should live in unity and good treatment of one another. "One mind" speaks of having the same outlook and purpose. "Compassionate" describes those who feel the pain of others. "Loving one another as brothers" means loving each other like siblings. "Tenderhearted" describes those with a gentle heart, and "courteous" (in other versions, "humble") points to kind and approachable treatment. Some ancient manuscripts have a different word at this last point, which is why the translations vary.

Peter, an apostle of Jesus, writes to scattered Christians who were suffering rejection because of their faith. After giving advice to wives and husbands, he closes with an invitation to the whole community. The verses that follow ask not to return evil for evil, but to bless.

For today: think of someone with whom you have tension and do something concrete this week, such as listening to them patiently, offering them help, or saying a kind word to them.
exp.0:18:
It says we were ransomed at a very high price: the precious blood of Christ, who is compared to a lamb without defect. The words "without blemish" and "without spot" mean that Jesus was free from sin and was perfect. "Ransomed" means set free by paying a price, as was done for a slave.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians who were living as foreigners and going through trials. He reminds them that their salvation was not bought with gold or silver, which perish, but with the giving up of Christ. Many understand the image of the lamb as an echo of the sacrifices of the Old Testament, especially the Passover. Peter uses it to encourage them to live with reverence.

For today: when you feel of little worth or find it hard to let go of old habits, remember that God paid an enormous price for you. Live with gratitude and reverence, not with fear, trusting that your worth does not depend on your achievements or your possessions.
exp.3:3:
This verse says that the believers' former friends are surprised to see that they no longer join them in a life without restraint. The phrase "the same excess of riot" means a total disorder, without control, in pleasures and excesses. The word "speaking evil of you" means that they insult them or speak badly of them for having changed.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians who suffered rejection in the midst of a pagan society. He reminds them that they already lived as everyone else did, and that now they follow the will of God. Their change causes surprise and mockery, but Peter tells them that God will judge everyone at the end.

Today, if you decide to live differently because of your faith, you may be criticized or others may pull away from you. Do not respond with pride or anger. Continue with humility, kindness, and firmness, trusting that God sees your effort and sustains you.
exp.4:11:
Peter says he wrote this short letter through Silvanus, whom he calls a faithful brother. The phrase "as I suppose" shows that Peter has a good opinion of him. The word "exhorting" means encouraging and warning you. Peter affirms that his message confirms the true grace of God, and he asks them to stand firm in it.

Peter writes to Christians who were suffering because of their faith. Silvanus may have been the secretary who wrote the letter, or perhaps the one who carried it; scholars interpret it in both ways. Peter closes his letter by reminding them of the essentials: suffering does not mean that God has abandoned them, for the grace of God remains upon them.

Today, when we go through difficult moments, let us not measure God's love by our circumstances. Let us stand firm in his grace, and encourage one another with simple and faithful words.
exp.0:22:
It says that believers have been born again, but not from a seed that decays or runs out, but from one that never rots. That seed is the word of God, which is living and lasts forever. "Born again" means born anew, and the "perishable seed" refers to human life, which wears out and comes to an end.

The apostle Peter writes to scattered Christians who were going through trials. He has just asked them to love one another deeply, that is, with heartfelt and sincere affection. Now he gives the reason: their new life comes from God and is not fragile. The verses that follow compare human life to grass that withers, while the word of the Lord remains. That word is the gospel they heard.

For today: when you feel weak or insecure, remember that your life in Christ rests on something firm. Nourish that life by reading the Bible every day, and love other believers sincerely.
exp.1:4:
It says that believers are like living stones that God is placing to form a spiritual house. We are also a holy priesthood, that is, people set apart for God. Our spiritual sacrifices are things like praise, service, and an obedient life. Being "built up" means that God himself is building us. Being "acceptable to God" means that they are pleasing to him, and this comes through Jesus Christ, because he is the way.

The apostle Peter is writing to scattered Christians, who were often rejected because of their faith. He has just spoken of Jesus as the living stone, rejected by people but chosen and precious to God. Peter reminds them that, although the world may look down on them, they belong to that same house and have value and purpose before God.

For today: do not live your faith alone. Find a church, serve it, and offer God your everyday life, your work, and your gratitude, knowing that you are part of what he is building.
exp.1:19:
It says there is no credit in enduring a punishment you earned by doing wrong. "Buffeted" means struck or mistreated, and "ye take it patiently" means you bear it with patience. By contrast, if someone does good, is mistreated without deserving it, and bears it with patience, that is pleasing to God. "Afflicted" means made to suffer.

Peter writes to Christians who were living as strangers among people who distrusted them. Here he speaks to servants, that is, to those who worked under masters, and some of those masters were harsh. He asks for a blameless witness, and right away points to Christ as the example of one who suffered without having done wrong. He does not say that injustice is good.

For today: if you are treated unfairly at work or at home, do not respond with revenge or deceit. Keep doing good calmly, and ask God for wisdom to know when to speak and when to seek help.
exp.3:0:
It says that Christ suffered physically for us, and that believers should prepare themselves with that same attitude, like someone putting on armor. "Be armed" means get ready, be prepared. "Has ceased from sin" means that whoever has suffered in the body for following Christ has broken with sin.

Peter writes to Christians who were suffering rejection and mockery for not living the way their pagan neighbors did. He wants to encourage them to see suffering as part of following Jesus. Interpreters explain the phrase "has ceased from sin" in several ways: some think that pain purifies, others that whoever chooses to suffer rather than sin has already broken with sin.

Today, when doing what is right costs you a mockery, a loss, or discomfort, do not take it as failure. Prepare your mind with the example of Christ and decide to obey God even when it costs you.
exp.0:23:
It says that every human being is fragile, like the grass of the field. Even what people take pride in, their fame, strength or success (the "glory" of man), lasts only a short time, like a flower that fades. The sentence about the old wording is removed here, since the phrases it explains do not appear in the verse your reader sees; the verse says the grass withers and the flower falls away, which means the flower drops off and disappears.

Peter writes to Christians who were scattered and suffering for their faith. He quotes Isaiah 40:6-8 to contrast two things: human life, which passes away, and the word of God, which endures. That is why he speaks earlier of a new birth through an imperishable seed. His point is to encourage them to love one another and to trust in what does not come to an end.

Today we can ask ourselves where we are placing our security: prestige, money or health do not last. Set aside time each day to read the Bible and to rely on God, whose word does not fail.
exp.0:12:
This verse says that, because of everything God has already done and revealed, we should prepare our minds. Gathering up the robe with a belt so one could move without hindrance is the picture behind the phrase in the original. Self-control and calmness are what the word for sobriety points to. To set your hope completely, without doubting, on the grace that will be given to us when Jesus Christ returns is what the verse means.

Peter writes to scattered Christians who were suffering for their faith. Earlier he spoke to them about the salvation that the prophets announced and that even the angels long to look into. Now, for that very reason, he calls them to live with a clear, alert mind and with their gaze fixed on Christ.

For today: take care of what feeds your mind. Before you react to problems with fear or anger, pause, pray, and remember that your hope rests on the grace of Christ, not on your circumstances.
exp.1:11:
This verse says that believers should live a good and upright life among those who do not know God. "Conduct" here means behavior or way of living, and "upright" means good and worthy. Even though they are accused of doing wrong, their good works could lead some to honor God "in the day of visitation." That phrase is difficult: many understand it as the moment when God visits those people to save them, and others as the day of final judgment.

The apostle Peter speaks to scattered Christians, treated as foreigners and looked down on for their faith. He reminds them that they are now God's people and asks them to live in such a way that their conduct answers the slander against them.

For today: when someone speaks badly of you for being a believer, do not defend yourself with anger. Respond with honesty, service, and steady kindness. Over time, your life can speak more loudly than the criticism.
exp.4:10:
He says that glory and dominion belong to God, that is, honor and the power to rule, and that this will be so forever. "Dominion" means authority or rule. "Amen" means "so be it" or "it is true."

Peter writes to Christians who were suffering for their faith. He has just told them that the suffering is temporary and that God himself will strengthen them. At the end of that promise, Peter responds with a brief song of praise: the God who sustains his people is the one who reigns over all.

When you go through a difficulty, do not just stare at the problem. Stop and praise God for who he is: he is in control and does not let go of you. That praise, even a simple one, reminds you that your suffering does not have the final word.
exp.4:1:
This verse says that the elders, or leaders of the church, are to shepherd God's flock, that is, to feed, guide and care for it the way a shepherd cares for his sheep. The word flock is what the verse calls God's people. They are to do this without being forced, but of their own free will. Doing it for dishonest gain means seeking money in the wrong way, and serving with a ready mind means having a heart that is willing and eager.

Peter writes to Christians who were facing pressure and trouble because of their faith. He presents himself as an elder alongside the other leaders, and as a witness of the sufferings of Christ. He does not speak from above, but as a fellow elder. He wants to encourage the leaders to serve well in difficult times, reminding them that the true Shepherd is Christ.

If you serve in the church, in a group, or even in your family, ask yourself why you do it. Try to serve with joy, not out of obligation, for money, or for recognition, but out of love for the people God has placed in your care.
exp.4:8:
This verse tells us to stand against the devil, the adversary mentioned in the verse before, by remaining firm in the faith. The word "resist" here means to stand against or oppose. The phrase "are accomplished" means that these sufferings are being lived through, or are being completed, in other believers. In other words, we are not the only ones who suffer.

Peter writes to scattered Christians who were facing trials and rejection because of their faith. Earlier he told them to cast their worries on God, because he cares for them, and to stay alert. Now he promises that God himself will strengthen them after a little suffering. Scholars debate how intense the persecution was at that time, but the comfort is clear.

For today: when you go through a trial, do not isolate yourself. Talk with other believers, ask for prayer, and remember that many brothers and sisters are also struggling. Stay firm, trusting in God.
exp.1:13:
This verse says that we should also respect governors, because the king sends them to punish those who do evil and to recognize those who do good. "Punishment" here means a just penalty, and "praise" means commendation or approval.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians who live as strangers in a world that often looked at them with suspicion. He asks them to live so good a life that the accusations against them fall away on their own. Submitting to the authorities is a way of honoring God and of showing that the Christian faith is not a threat. Some believe Peter speaks in a general way about government, and others see it applied to their particular situation.

Today, we can obey the laws, pay our taxes, and treat authorities with respect. In this way, our good witness speaks for us, even when we do not agree on everything.
exp.3:13:
If someone insults or looks down on you for being a follower of Christ, it says you should not feel defeated but blessed. "Reproached" means insulted or harshly criticized. "Happy" means blessed, joyful, favored by God. The Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you, meaning God is especially with you. The last clause says that those who mock speak evil of Christ, but your faithfulness honors him. Some early manuscripts do not include that last clause.

Peter writes to scattered Christians who were facing rejection and pressure because of their faith. He wants to encourage them not to be surprised by the trial, and he reminds them that suffering for Christ unites them to him. The verses that follow clarify that this suffering is for following Christ, not for doing wrong.

For today: if someone mocks your faith, respond with calm and kindness, without returning insult, remembering that God is with you.
exp.0:4:
It says that believers are "kept", that is, guarded and protected by the power of God, as under the watch of a guard, and that this protection is received through faith. The purpose is to reach salvation, which here means complete salvation. That salvation is already prepared and ready, and it will be revealed openly in the last time, the final time.

The apostle Peter writes to scattered Christians who were suffering trials and rejection. Earlier he spoke of the inheritance kept in heaven; now he shows that the heirs are also kept. He wants to encourage them: their suffering is temporary, and their future is secure in the hands of God.

For today: when you feel weak or are going through a trial, remember that your salvation does not depend on your strength but on the power of God. Trust Him with simple faith, one day at a time, and rest in the knowledge that He sustains you to the end.
exp.1:7:
The verse says that Christ, the stone God set as the foundation, is also a stone over which some stumble. Those people stumble because they do not obey the word. "Stumbling block" here means an obstacle that makes a person fall. The final phrase, "for which they were also appointed," is understood in different ways: some believe it speaks of God having already determined the fate of those who disobey; others, that God arranged for whoever rejects Christ to stumble over Him.

Peter is writing to Christians scattered abroad who were suffering rejection because of their faith. He quotes the Old Testament (Isaiah 28:16; Psalm 118:22; Isaiah 8:14) to show them that the rejection of Jesus had already been foretold. Believers receive honor; unbelievers, stumbling.

For today: if faith in Christ brings you mockery or misunderstanding, remember that you are not failing. Stand firm and obey his word with humility, knowing that God sustains you.
exp.1:15:
They say that Christians are truly free, but that they must not use that freedom as an excuse or a disguise for doing wrong. "Cloak of maliciousness" means a kind of mask that hides an evil intention. Instead, they must live as "servants of God," that is, people who belong to Him and want to obey Him.

The apostle Peter writes to scattered believers who lived as foreigners in a world that looked at them with suspicion. He asks them to respect the authorities and, through their good conduct, to refute the false accusations. Their freedom in Christ does not make them rebels; it makes them accountable to God.

For today: before saying "I am free to do this," ask yourself whether that freedom serves to love and do good, or whether it only hides selfishness. Live your freedom with respect, honesty, and a desire to please God.
exp.0:24:
It says that the word of the Lord "endureth for ever," meaning it lasts forever and never loses its worth. Peter contrasts it with grass and flowers, which wither and fall. Then he clarifies which word he means: the gospel, the message of good news that was preached to them, that is, proclaimed and made known.

Peter writes to Christians who were scattered and probably going through trials. He reminds them that they have been born again through the word of God, not through something temporary. He quotes Isaiah 40:6-8, where the prophet encouraged a weary people to trust what God says. In this way Peter invites them to place their hope in something certain.

Today we live among news, trends, and opinions that change quickly. We can choose a fixed time each day to read a passage of the gospel and rest our decisions and our encouragement on it, because what God has said still stands.
exp.4:4:
This verse says that younger people should be respectful toward the elders, meaning the leaders of the church. Then it asks everyone to serve one another with humility. The phrase about putting on humility is like someone putting on clothing, wearing humility as a garment. The proud are those who think highly of themselves, and grace is the undeserved favor of God.

Peter is writing to Christians who are under pressure because of their faith. Just before this, he asked the elders to care for the flock by example and not by domination. Now he turns to the younger members. Some understand "elders" to mean leaders and others to mean older people; it may include both meanings. The central point is that everyone practices humility.

For today: this week, listen carefully to someone older or to a leader in your church, and serve another person without seeking recognition. Humility opens the door to the grace of God.
exp.1:10:
Peter calls the believers "dearly beloved" and urges them with affection. He calls them "strangers and pilgrims," that is, people who live in this world but do not belong to it. He asks them to stay away from "fleshly lusts," the urges of selfishness and sin, which "war against the soul," meaning they fight against our spiritual life. The call to "abstain" means to keep yourselves far away.

Peter writes to scattered Christians who felt out of place in their society. Earlier he reminded them that they are now God's people. From that new identity he asks them to live a clean life, so that non-believers, who were criticizing them, will see their good works and glorify God.

For today: when a desire comes that would harm your heart or your relationships, remember who you are in Christ. Before giving in, pause, pray, and choose one good and concrete action in its place.
exp.2:20:
This verse says that baptism is a "figure," or image, that corresponds to the water of the flood in Noah's time. Just as the ark carried eight people safely through the water, baptism saves us, but not because it washes dirt off the body. What matters is the appeal of a good conscience toward God, that is, a sincere response, a commitment or plea from a clear conscience. All of this happens through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians who are suffering for their faith. He reminds them that Noah, though he was in the minority, was kept safe by God. Interpreters explain in different ways how baptism works in salvation, but they all agree that the power lies in the risen Christ, not in the water.

Today, do not trust in a ritual as if it were a charm. Live your baptism with sincerity: ask God for a clear conscience, and rely every day on the victory of Jesus.
exp.2:19:
This verse speaks of the people who were disobedient in the days of Noah. God waited patiently while Noah was building the ark. Only eight people were saved through the water.

Peter writes to Christians who were suffering because of their faith. He reminds them that Christ also suffered though he was righteous, and that God prevailed in the end. Who the "imprisoned spirits" are is interpreted in several ways, and Christians do not agree on a single explanation. Peter uses Noah as an example: few were saved, but God took care of them.

Today, if you feel like a minority for following Christ, remember that God is patient and faithful. Trust in Him, even if others do not.
exp.0:0:
Peter introduces himself as an apostle of Jesus Christ, that is, someone sent with the authority of Jesus. He writes to "strangers scattered throughout" several regions of what is today Turkey: Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia. The word "scattered" means spread out across different places.

Peter, one of the twelve disciples, writes to Christians who lived far from their homeland or who felt out of place in their society. It is not known with certainty whether they were Jews, Gentiles, or both; scholars see this in different ways. What the letter does show is that they faced hardships, and Peter wants to encourage them by reminding them who they are before God.

Even when you feel out of place because of your faith, your identity does not depend on where you live or on whether others accept you. God knows you and calls you his own. Today, rest in that.
exp.3:15:
If someone suffers for being a Christian, he says, they should not feel ashamed. On the contrary, they should give glory to God for bearing that name. "Suffers" means undergoes hardship, "ashamed" means feeling disgrace or dishonor, and "in this matter" is understood as "in this case" or "for this reason."

Peter writes to Christians who were living as strangers in the world and were criticized or mistreated because of their faith. Before this verse, he distinguishes between suffering for doing wrong, which brings no honor, and suffering for following Christ, which brings the presence of the Spirit. He reminds them that the name "Christian" was a reason for mockery, but before God it is a reason for honor.

Today, if someone mocks you or pushes you to the margins because of your faith, do not hide or feel lesser. Respond with respect, with good conduct, and by giving thanks to God for belonging to him.
exp.2:10:
It says that whoever wants to live well must turn away from what is evil and do what is good. They must also seek peace and pursue it, that is, make real effort to achieve it. The phrase "turn away" means "let him turn away," and "pursue it" means "let him go after it" and not give up.

Peter writes to Christians who were suffering rejection and mockery because of their faith. He asks them not to repay evil with evil, but to respond with blessing. This verse continues a quotation from Psalm 34, which Peter uses to show how someone who trusts God lives. He then makes clear that God cares for the righteous and hears them.

For today: when someone treats you badly, do not answer in the same way. Think before you speak, and take a concrete step toward peace, such as offering a kind word or being the first to ask forgiveness. Peace almost never comes on its own; you have to go after it.
exp.1:8:
