This verse says that believers in Christ are a family chosen by God, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, and a people that God has made his own. "Family line" means family or descendants; "a people set apart for God" is a people set apart for God; "a people God claimed as his own" is a people God took as his own. All of this is so that they may proclaim the excellencies, that is, the works and admirable character of God, who called them out of darkness into his marvelous light.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians who are scattered and at times mistreated because of their faith. Earlier he spoke of Christ as the stone rejected by some and precious to those who believe. Now he reminds them of their identity: even though the world may despise them, God has chosen them and honored them. With these ancient words about Israel, Peter describes the church.

For today: remember that your worth comes from what God says about you, not from the rejection of others. This week, simply tell someone something good that God has done in your life.
exp.0:6:
This verse says that the trials believers face serve to show that their faith is genuine. Faith is worth more than gold, which in the end wears away, even when it is refined by fire. When Jesus Christ is revealed, that is, when he is shown to everyone at his return, this tested faith will receive praise, glory, and honor.

The apostle Peter writes to scattered Christians who were suffering affliction, probably because of their faith. He does not want them to lose heart. He reminds them that God keeps them and that their present suffering is temporary. Scholars debate what kind of persecution it was, but the encouraging purpose of the letter is clear.

When you go through a difficulty, do not think that God has forgotten you. Ask him to use that trial to strengthen your confidence in him. A faith that holds firm is worth more than anything you could lose.
exp.3:2:
It says that the time already passed in our lives, when we lived like those who do not know God, is enough. "Lasciviousness" refers to unrestrained sexual excess; "lusts" refers to disordered desires; "gluttony" and "banquets" refer to drunken feasts and parties without control. "Gentiles" were the peoples who did not follow the God of Israel.

The apostle Peter writes to Christians who were suffering mockery and rejection in several regions. They had come out of a pagan way of life, and their former friends did not understand why they no longer joined them. Peter encourages them to think as Christ did, who suffered for doing what was right, and to live for the will of God.

Today we can ask ourselves which habits of the past still pull at us. With God's help, let us make a concrete decision: to stay away from a place or a custom that harms us, even though others may be puzzled.
exp.4:12:
Peter sends greetings from the church that is in Babylon, which, like the readers of the letter, was chosen by God. Mark also sends greetings. Peter calls him "my son," a loving way of speaking about someone whom he guided in the faith.

Peter writes to Christians who are scattered and going through hardship, and he closes his letter with greetings. Many think that "Babylon" is a symbolic name for Rome, but others believe it refers to the actual city in Mesopotamia. There is no complete certainty. This Mark is usually identified with John Mark, the author of the Gospel, although the letter does not make this clear.

Today, this verse reminds us that no church stands alone. Even when we live far away or in difficult settings, we are part of a family chosen by God. Today you can encourage another believer with a message or a prayer.
exp.3:5:
It says that the gospel was also preached to "the dead," that is, to people who had already died when it was preached to them or who died after hearing it. Its purpose is twofold: that according to men they might be judged "in the flesh" (suffering physical death, as all do), but that according to God they might live "in the spirit." "Preached" means announced; the old spelling "á" is the older way of writing "a."

Peter writes to Christians who suffer mockery and rejection for leaving behind the disordered life they once lived. He reminds them that God will judge the living and the dead. Interpreters explain this verse in several ways: the most common is that it speaks of believers who had already died and who had heard the gospel during their lives. Other readings are more debated.

For today: do not be discouraged if others criticize you for following Christ. Human judgment is temporary; what matters is living for God, with a hope that death does not extinguish.
exp.2:9:
This verse says that whoever wants to enjoy life and see good days must take care with what they say. They must hold back their tongue from speaking evil, and keep their lips from speaking deceit.

Here the apostle Peter is speaking to Christians who were suffering rejection and mistreatment because of their faith. He has just asked them not to answer evil with evil, but with a blessing. To support his teaching, he quotes Psalm 34, which connects a good life with clean and sincere words.

Today, before we respond in anger, whether online or at home, we can stop for a moment and choose words that are true and kind. Asking God for help to speak this way is a good place to start.
exp.1:12:
They say that believers should submit to every human authority, not out of fear or convenience, but out of respect for God. The phrase translated here as "every ordinance of man" refers to the institutions or laws that people set up. To submit means to place yourself under authority with a good attitude. The "king" was the Roman emperor, whom the verse calls "supreme" because he held the highest office.

The one speaking is the apostle Peter, and he writes to Christians scattered abroad who were living as strangers in the midst of people who did not believe. Many looked at them with suspicion and accused them of doing wrong. Peter wants their good conduct, even toward the authorities, to leave their critics without arguments and to honor God.

For today: fulfill your civic duties, such as paying taxes and respecting the laws, doing so wholeheartedly and with honesty. In this way your conduct can be a quiet testimony of your faith.
exp.4:2:
This verse says that the leaders of the church must not rule harshly or think of themselves as owners of the people. "Being lords over" means controlling others as a master would. "God's heritage" refers to the people who belong to God, his own people. "Ensamples" means examples or models. "Flock" is the herd, the congregation.

Peter speaks to the elders, that is, to the leaders of the churches, and includes himself among them as an elder too. He writes to Christians who were under pressure and hardship. He reminds them that the people are not theirs but God's, and that Jesus is the true Chief Shepherd.

For today: if you guide others, whether in the church, in your family, or in a group, let your example speak more than your orders. Treat people with respect, knowing that they are precious to God.
exp.3:6:
It says that the end of all things is near. For this reason it asks readers to be sober, that is, sensible, self-controlled and balanced. It also asks them to watch unto prayer, meaning to stay awake and alert, speaking with God.

Peter wrote to first-century Christians who suffered rejection because of their faith. He has just spoken of God's judgment. Interpreters explain "the end" in several ways: the coming of Christ, the final judgment, or the time close to these events. In any case, Peter wants them to live with calm and hope, and right away he calls them to love one another and to be hospitable.

For today: set aside a fixed moment each day to pray quietly, before the noise and the rush. Ask God for clarity to decide wisely and to love better those who are near you.
exp.0:7:
They say that believers love Jesus even though they have never seen him with their eyes. They believe in him without seeing him now, and so they rejoice with a joy that is "unspeakable," that is, so great that it cannot be explained in words. Moreover, he is "full of glory," meaning full of a greatness that comes from God.

The apostle Peter writes to scattered Christians who were suffering various trials. Shortly before, he told them that their faith, more precious than gold, is tested like gold in the fire. After this he speaks of "the salvation of your souls," which means being saved. Peter encourages them to look beyond the present pain, toward the day when Jesus will be revealed.

For today: even though you do not see Christ, your love and your trust in him are real. On a difficult day, take a few minutes to thank him for what he has already done, and ask him to give you his joy in the middle of the trial.
exp.4:0:
Peter speaks with warmth to the elders, that is, to the leaders and pastors of the churches. The word "I exhort" means "I urge" or "I appeal earnestly." He places himself alongside them: he is "an elder also." He says he was "a witness of the sufferings of Christ," since he saw his suffering, and that he will also share in the glory that God will reveal when Christ returns.

The writer is the apostle Peter, speaking from a position of authority but without imposing himself. He writes to Christians who were under pressure and rejection, and before giving instructions to the leaders (in the verses that follow), he presents himself as a companion, not as a boss. Some think "witness" refers to the fact that he saw it personally; others, that it also speaks of his own suffering for Christ.

For today: if you guide or teach others, do so with humility, like someone who walks alongside them and who hopes for the same glory they do.
exp.0:19:
He says that Christ, the spotless Lamb of the previous verse, was already appointed or chosen by God before the creation of the world. But he was made known in these last times, meaning the final times, which the Bible uses for the era that began with Christ's coming. The word "manifest" means shown openly. And all of it was for your sake: for you.

Peter, an apostle of Jesus, writes to scattered Christians who were suffering for their faith. He reminds them that they were redeemed with the blood of Christ, not with gold or silver. He wants them to see that their salvation was not an improvised plan, but a firm purpose of God. This encourages them to live with faith and hope.

For today: when you feel small, forgotten, or insecure, remember that God thought of you and of your redemption before anything else existed. Respond with gratitude, trusting in him and loving others sincerely.
exp.1:21:
This verse says that Jesus never committed sin and that he never lied or deceived anyone with his words. The phrase about being found is explained as: although they examined him, no fault was found in him. "Mouth" stands for everything he said.

Peter writes to Christians who were suffering injustice, perhaps as servants or living among hostile people. He tells them that suffering for doing good is pleasing to God. Peter uses Christ as the example: he suffered while being innocent. The verse partly quotes Isaiah 53:9, which speaks of the suffering servant.

Today, when someone treats us badly without reason, we can look to Jesus. He teaches us to respond with truth and without revenge, trusting that God is just. Let us also take care with our words: may they be sincere and free of deception.
exp.2:2:
This verse says that the beauty of believing women should not depend on outward things: elaborate hairstyles, gold jewelry, and flashy clothing. It does not forbid getting dressed up or taking care of one's appearance; it simply says that these should not be the most important thing.

Peter writes to Christians who were under pressure in a world that did not believe. Here he speaks to wives whose husbands did not yet believe. He tells them that their pure and respectful conduct could speak more powerfully than arguments. Many understand the contrast to be with vanity and the desire to show off, since the following verse speaks about the heart.

For today: take care of your appearance with simplicity, but invest more time in cultivating a character that is kind, patient, and sincere. That also applies to men.

sum.1: Peter invites believers to put aside all wickedness and grow in their relationship with God. Christ, the living stone, makes them a holy people who proclaim his excellencies. He asks them to live well, to respect those in authority, and to endure unjust suffering as Christ did, who bore our sins and healed us, and to return to him as our Shepherd.
sum.4: Peter urges the elders to take care of God's people willingly and by setting a good example, not for money or by bossing people around, and he promises that the Chief Shepherd will reward them. To everyone he teaches to clothe themselves in humility, to leave their worries with God, to stay alert against the devil, and to resist him by standing firm in the faith. After a little suffering, God will strengthen them.
sum.3: Peter encourages believers to live according to God's will and not as they did before, even though others reject them for it. He calls them to love one another deeply, to be hospitable, and to serve others with the gifts they have, so that God may be glorified. If they suffer for being Christians, they should not be ashamed, but should entrust their lives to the faithful Creator and keep doing good.
sum.2: Peter teaches wives and husbands to live with respect, inner beauty, and mutual honor, and he calls everyone to love, kindness, and blessing toward those who do them wrong. He encourages believers not to fear if they suffer for doing good, and to give an account of their hope with gentleness. Christ suffered for us, rose again, and reigns in heaven.
sum.0: Peter writes to Christians who are scattered and suffering, reminding them that God has given them new birth into a living hope and an inheritance kept safe for them in heaven. Even though they face trials, their faith is worth more than gold. He calls them to live holy lives, because they were redeemed by the precious blood of Christ, and to love one another from the heart.
